key_insight: Pretrained protein language models (pLMs) can introduce data leakage into protein–protein interaction (PPI) inference pipelines, causing artificially inflated evaluation scores that overstate real predictive ability.
problem_solved: Identifies and diagnoses a hidden source of overestimation in PPI prediction: using pretrained pLM embeddings without leakage-aware controls can leak information across train/test partitions and distort model evaluation.
method: Analyze how pretrained pLM-derived features can carry information that bridges training and test sets in common PPI setups.
Run comparative experiments showing performance differences between standard pipelines and leakage-controlled evaluation (e.g., stricter splitting or feature masking).
Propose/illustrate evaluation best practices and ablations to isolate true model generalization from pLM-induced leakage.
impact: Alerts ML and bioinformatics practitioners that off-the-shelf pLM embeddings may compromise the validity of PPI benchmarks; adopting leakage-aware evaluation prevents misleading conclusions and improves model reliability.
visual_elements: Flow diagram showing how pLM embeddings are produced and where leakage can cross train/test boundaries
Bar chart comparing reported performance (standard pipeline) vs corrected performance (leakage-controlled) to visualize inflation
Schematic of evaluation protocols: standard split vs leakage-aware split (with clear partitioning rules)
Checklist/infographic panel of recommended practices (e.g., split rules, embedding controls, ablation steps)
paper_title: A flaw in using pretrained protein language models in protein–protein interaction inference models
